title: Existence of pairwise maximin-share allocations
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal:
Does every finite instance of indivisible goods and nonnegative additive valuations admit a complete pairwise maximin-share allocation? Precisely, for all integers \(n\ge1\), \(m\ge0\), and every matrix \(v\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times m}\), is there a partition \((A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) of the goods such that
\[
\forall i,j\in[n],\ i\ne j:\quad
v_i(A_i)\ge\mu_i(A_i\cup A_j,2),
\]
with the two-part maximin value \(\mu_i\) defined below? This preserves the exact existence question from Open Problem 8 of the 2022 survey. It is a historical question now answered negatively; no approximation or epistemic variant is substituted.
why: The question asked whether a demanding pairwise fairness guarantee could always be achieved when resources cannot be divided. It connected two-person maximin guarantees with fairness across a larger society and with stronger versus weaker envy conditions. The negative resolution establishes a limitation of this exact guarantee even for three agents and strictly positive additive values.
status_note: Resolved negatively by September 2026 preprints. The checked three-agent, nine-good positive-integer instance in Gölz arXiv:2609.08954v1 refutes the survey’s universal additive-goods existence statement. This review read the complete nonexistence proof and independently verified all 19,683 complete allocations using exact arithmetic. The cited works are recent preprints; the review does not claim peer-reviewed publication or a Lean-checked proof. The original question is archived with its complete record preserved.

progress.text: The checked survey revision states the additive setting in Section 1.1 and leaves universal PMMS existence open as Open Problem 8.
Aziz announces a four-agent counterexample with strictly positive additive valuations to complete PMMS existence in Theorem 1.
Gölz gives a three-agent, nine-good positive-integer instance in Section 2 and proves its lack of any PMMS allocation in Theorem 1 and Lemmas 1–2.
Bei, Lin, Liu, Luan and Tao also prove nonexistence for additive goods in Theorem 3, using a reduction connecting the chores and goods settings.

Individual review matched the original complete-allocation question to the three-agent counterexample, read the complete nonexistence proof, and independently checked every one of its 19,683 allocations and all relevant two-part partitions with exact arithmetic. The full card was prepared for retirement as resolved.

sentences: The historical question asks whether every collection of indivisible goods with nonnegative additive valuations admits a complete PMMS allocation.
Each agent must receive at least her best two-part maximin guarantee within the union of her bundle and any other agent’s bundle.
A September 2026 counterexample uses only three agents, nine goods and strictly positive integer values.
The complete nonexistence proof and an independent exact enumeration of all allocations were checked against the original target.
The question is therefore archived as resolved negatively, with its original record preserved.

definitions:
The agents are \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the goods are \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). Each number \(v_{ig}\) is a finite nonnegative real value assigned by agent \(i\) to good \(g\). Additivity means
\[
v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\quad(S\subseteq[m]),
\qquad v_i(\varnothing)=0.
\]
There is no assumption that agents have identical values, that their total values agree, or that singleton values are positive rather than merely nonnegative.

A complete allocation assigns every good to exactly one agent: the bundles \(A_i\subseteq[m]\) are pairwise disjoint and their union is \([m]\). Empty bundles are permitted. Goods cannot be divided, shared or left unallocated, and there are no transfers or extra feasibility constraints.

For any \(S\subseteq[m]\), define
\[
\mu_i(S,2)=
\max_{T\subseteq S}\min\{v_i(T),v_i(S\setminus T)\}.
\]
Both parts may be empty. The maximum is over a nonempty finite collection, so it is attained even when \(S=\varnothing\). Both parts are evaluated by the same agent \(i\). An allocation is pairwise maximin-share fair, abbreviated PMMS, if the displayed inequality in the formal statement holds for every ordered pair of distinct agents. It compares each agent's own bundle to the best two-way guarantee within the actual two agents' combined bundles. It does not impose a maximin benchmark on all goods or allow an alternative allocation to be chosen separately for each comparison.

The question is mathematical existence, with no computation-time, oracle, uniformity or input-encoding restriction. Real-valued instances are included. A finite integer-valued counterexample is also an instance in this domain.
answer_criterion:
A benchmark answer would be a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the universal existence statement or its negation. A positive answer would establish a complete PMMS allocation for every allowed \(n,m,v\). A negative answer must give some finite \(n,m,v\) and prove that every map \(h:[m]\to[n]\), with bundles \(A_i=h^{-1}(\{i\})\), has distinct agents \(i,j\) and a subset \(T\subseteq A_i\cup A_j\) satisfying
\[
v_i(A_i)<
\min\{v_i(T),v_i((A_i\cup A_j)\setminus T)\}.
\]
This is the full negation of existence for that instance. The published finite counterexample resolves the historical mathematical question, but this review does not claim that its proof or the separate computational audit has already been checked in Lean.

context_blocks.text: Pairwise maximin-share fairness considers the actual union of two agents’ bundles. For each ordered pair, the first agent must receive at least the value she could guarantee by partitioning that union into two bundles and accepting the less valuable one. Completeness matters: permitting goods to be discarded would change the existence question.

The original survey focuses on additive nonnegative valuations and asks universal PMMS existence. This differs from asking whether a particular instance has such an allocation, from approximate PMMS, and from epistemic PMMS, which changes the comparison allocation. Those are separate mathematical targets.

With strictly positive singleton values, PMMS implies envy-freeness up to any removed good: an agent does not prefer another bundle after any one good is removed from it. A counterexample to the stronger PMMS requirement does not by itself refute the weaker envy-freeness requirement.

September 2026 preprints refute universal PMMS existence for additive goods. Gölz provides a three-agent, nine-good instance with strictly positive integer values and a proof covering all allocations. The review checked that concrete instance and its proof and independently exhausted all complete allocations using exact integer arithmetic. The original problem is therefore retired with its full record retained.

checked_sources: Read the entire original canonical TCS-1119 and the actual saved primary PDF, which is arXiv2202.07551v2 dated 4 March 2022, 17 pages, by Amanatidis, Birmpas, Filos-Ratsikas and Voudouris. Section 1.1 p2 explicitly sets nonnegative real additive values and complete partitions; PMMS is defined across pp7–8 and Open Problem 8 on p8 asks whether an allocation always exists. The original author list is correct for this version and must not be replaced by the eight-author 2023 survey cited in newer papers.

Downloaded and read actual Gölz arXiv2609.08954v1, submitted 8 September 2026, and checked arXiv history displaying only v1. Definition 1 p1 exactly matches the pairwise max-min inequality, with no epistemic relaxation or disposability. The three-agent/nine-good integer table on p2 has strictly positive entries and therefore lies inside the survey’s nonnegative-real domain. A counterexample for this subclass refutes the universal target without any encoding or complexity assumption.

Read the full human-readable Theorem 1 proof on pp2–7, including the facts forcing one large good and a small good per agent, the two partitions P/Q, the makeweight contradiction and all case distinctions in Lemmas 1 and 2. Checked the resulting covers of possible small-good patterns and the displayed numerical inequalities against the table. The proof addresses every complete allocation. The public historical card records the resolution without reproducing proof strategies or a new optimization target.

Independently implemented research/random-card-review-20260914/pmms-counterexample-audit.py from the mathematical definition, rather than executing the paper’s supplied script. Precomputed every agent’s value on all 512 subsets and the exact max-min benchmark for every union by enumerating all submasks. Enumerated all 3^9=19683 ownership maps, including empty bundles, and checked all six ordered pairs. No allocation is PMMS. Exact rational ratios also reproduce 186/187 as the optimal approximation factor for this particular first table, attained at ownership vector (0,1,2,0,2,0,2,1,2). The JSON audit records the table, counts and a digest of one strict violating pair per allocation. No floating-point arithmetic was used, and no Lean verification is claimed.

Checked actual Aziz arXiv2609.06282v1 submitted 5 September 2026, its introductory definition and Theorem 1 p2. It independently announces a four-agent strictly positive additive counterexample; the construction and proof are located pp3–4 onward but were not the basis of the exhaustive verification here. Checked actual Bei–Lin–Liu–Luan–Tao arXiv2609.10493v1 submitted 9 September 2026, abstract, result overview and Theorem 3 p6, which explicitly includes additive-goods nonexistence. The additional NP-hardness and approximation theorems are not needed for this retirement and were not fully audited.

The recent epistemic-PMMS paper, arXiv2606.18921, concerns a relaxation with different witnessing allocations; its three-agent positive result does not contradict the exact PMMS counterexample. Likewise earlier negative results for general monotone valuations or chores alone would not have sufficed for this additive-goods question. The archival decision relies on the exact matching finite counterexample, not an abstract-only generalization of a differently scoped result.

A second independent reviewer read the original survey and the complete Gölz proof and found no scope or proof gap. A separate set-based verification checked all 19683 assignments, obtaining 78 EFX allocations and four surviving the necessary single-item-swap condition; all four violate PMMS by the supplied repartition. The bounded review, precise inspected sources and distinction from Lean verification are retained in research/random-card-review-20260914/pmms-independent-review.md.
